pr_title: disable caching for authoritative zone to comply with rfc-1035 section 6.1.2
pr_body:

#### What type of PR is this?
/kind bug

<!--
Add one of the following kinds:

/kind feature

Optionally add one or more of the following kinds if applicable:
/kind api-change
/kind deprecation
/kind failing-test
/kind flake
/kind regression
-->

#### What this PR does / why we need it:
It changes the kubernetes plugin configuration in the coredns Corefile to disable caching for the domain which the plugin is authoritative for.

Coredns delegates responsibility to plugins which it chains together. Currently a `cache` plugin is earlier in the chain than the `kubernetes` plugin. This combined with the current Corefile has undesirable consequences such as being slow to reflect changes in the environment and the possibility of providing conflicting responses around the time of a cache update.

Without this change coredns will be misconfigured according to RFC 1035 (6.1.2 name server implementation, database):
> With the proper search procedures, authoritative data in zones
     will always "hide", and hence take precedence over, cached
     data.

#### Which issue(s) this PR fixes:

IMO, it will reduce the performance of the coredns if we disable it.

Without this change coredns will be misconfigured according to RFC 1035 (6.1.2 name server implementation, database):
> With the proper search procedures, authoritative data in zones
     will always "hide", and hence take precedence over, cached
     data.

I think this is a good addition.  I have also recommended this configuration in the past to users concerned with cluster domain record lag induced by caching. This is better than setting the TTL to zero for all cluster domain responses since some clients may mishandle ttl 0 responses. 

It doesn’t avert caching of reverse zone answers produced by the Kubernetes plugin, but I think that’s ok for now.

A compelling alternate solution suggested by @matteriben is to change the order of plugin execution in the coredns build such that kubernetes comes before cache. This would also prevent the reverse zone responses from entering cache, but it’s a bigger change and may introduce backward incompatibility or other complications resulting from changing the Kubernetes plugin relative to other plugins (other than cache). … needs further thought and comparison with other potential solutions such as adding a mechanism for plugins to internally tag responses as authoritative so that cache can skip them.

For now, I think this configmap change solution is low risk and is good for inclusion as the default.

issue_context.title: Headless Service not publishing not ready addresses for statefulset
issue_context.body:
**What happened**:

Deploying a StatefulSet with a headless service and properly configured `spec.serviceName` doesn't publish the underlying pod's on the internal Kube-DNS for at least 30 seconds after pod creation, even if the headless service has explicit `publishNotReadyAddresses: true` and even if a pod has a `readinessProbe` of 1 second which shouldn't matter if the publishNotReadyAddresses is set to true according to [documentation](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/dns-pod-service/#pod-s-hostname-and-subdomain-fields) .

This causes that if the stateful application, which relies on a pod being able to communicate to it's peer for bootstrapping, doesn't start for at least 30 seconds due to this delay.

**What you expected to happen**:

I'm expecting the fully qualified names of the pods under the statefulset to become avaiable in the DNS so the pods in the statefulset can find it's own peers via their dns name (i.e. `pod-0.statefulset-svc` can connect to `pod-1.statefulset-svc`)

**How to reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)**:

I've designed a simple application that since starting it tries to ping it's own peers under the same application, you can clearly see that for the first 30 seconds of the pod existance, it cannot reach it's peers, not even itself, this is because the pod's name is not being announced in the internal KubeDNS.

Using the following statefulset you can observe the behavior:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  labels:
    app: minio
    controller: message-dist
  name: message-dist
  namespace: default
spec:
  clusterIP: None
  ports:
    - name: minio-port
      port: 8090
      protocol: TCP
      targetPort: 8090
  publishNotReadyAddresses: true
  selector:
    app: minio
    controller: message-dist
  sessionAffinity: None
  type: ClusterIP
---
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: StatefulSet
metadata:
  name: message-dist
  namespace: default
spec:
  podManagementPolicy: Parallel
  replicas: 4
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: minio
      controller: message-dist
  serviceName: message-dist
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: minio
        controller: message-dist
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: message
          command:
            - /message
            - http://message-dist-{0...3}.message-dist:8090/
          env:
            - name: MESSAGE
              valueFrom:
                fieldRef:
                  fieldPath: metadata.name
          image: dvaldivia/message:dist
#          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          imagePullPolicy: Always
          livenessProbe:
            failureThreshold: 3
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8090
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 1
            periodSeconds: 20
            successThreshold: 1
            timeoutSeconds: 1
          readinessProbe:
            failureThreshold: 3
            httpGet:
              path: /
              port: 8090
              scheme: HTTP
            initialDelaySeconds: 1
            periodSeconds: 20
            successThreshold: 1
            timeoutSeconds: 1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 8090
              name: minio-port
              protocol: TCP
          resources: {}
          volumeMounts:
            - mountPath: /data1
              name: data1
  updateStrategy:
    rollingUpdate:
      partition: 0
    type: RollingUpdate
  volumeClaimTemplates:
    - metadata:
        name: data1
      spec:
        accessModes:
          - ReadWriteOnce
        resources:
          requests:
            storage: 1Gi
```

Or simply apply this file:

```
kubectl apply -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/dvaldivia/message/master/message-dist.yaml
```

**Anything else we need to know?**:

This problem could be avoided if the Kube-DNS made the service subdomains for the pods available sooner than 30 seconds, I cannot find anywhere in the documentation where it specifies this 30 seconds delay.

**Environment**:
- Kubernetes version (use `kubectl version`):  `client 1.18.4 ` `server 1.18.2`
- Cloud provider or hardware configuration: kind, gke

Ahhhh  i see the issue, After some poking it became clear that
 
- The pods as you show are *clearly* up and running very quickly
- The time interval is religiously 30 seconds.
- To fix , just chance `cache 30` to something like `cache 5` in your coreDNS pods !

so, it turns out that by default, i think most of the time your CoreDNS is running the cache plugin with, you guessed it, *30* seconds for responses.  Thus, since your pod is querying before the other pods are up the first response is that 'i have no clue what pod this is ', and you'll never get positive respose until 30 seconds after the failed request.

The solution was simplee, 
```
- apiVersion: v1
  data:
    Corefile: |
      .:53 {
          errors
          health {
             lameduck 5s
          }
          ready
          kubernetes cluster.local in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa {
             pods insecure
             fallthrough in-addr.arpa ip6.arpa
             ttl 30
          }
          prometheus :9153
          forward . /etc/resolv.conf
          cache 5 # Change this field from cache 30 to cache 5 , and youll see the services come up rapidly 
          loop
          reload
          loadbalance
```
The way you edit this is by running `kubectl edit cm coredns -n kube-system` and then simple re running your test , you'll see an immediate improvement.

Looks like the NXDOMAIN ttl was changed to 30s in https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/76238 to be consistent with kube-dns config. However, kube-dns/dnsmasq does not cache NXDOMAIN at all. So, we should probably change this default back to 5s for NXDOMAIN responses? @chrisohaver @Deiken
@prameshj that would improve things a lot, I'd all in for no caching at all for NXDOMAIN

> @prameshj that would improve things a lot, I'd all in for no caching at all for NXDOMAIN

Not caching NXDOMAIN at all will make every single searchpath-expanded and AAAA queries to be processed by kubernetes plugin rather than returned from cache. These 2 are some of the significant sources of DNS traffic. Probably less of an issue for CoreDNS than kube-dns, but I would expect changing that value to result in some performance regression.

i made a note in the docs around this , that might be a reasonable action item for this

@dvaldivia any other ideas we should pursue ? Feel free to schedule a time to discuss again, you can ping me (jayunit100) on slack

> Looks like the NXDOMAIN ttl was changed to 30s in #76238 to be consistent with kube-dns config. However, kube-dns/dnsmasq does not cache NXDOMAIN at all. So, we should probably change this default back to 5s for NXDOMAIN responses? @chrisohaver @Deiken

The TTL control in the kubernetes plugin a single setting for all responses. So, 5s for all records, or 30s for all records.
We could cut the max cache time for negative responses to 5s for _all_ domains, but that would also affect upstream NXDOMAIN responses.

As far as disabling NXDOMAIN cache, negative cache (which includes NXDOMAIN and some other negative responses) can only be disabled globally (i.e. disabling caching of upstream NXDOMAINs).  The performance impact on fruitless search path expansions and AAAA queries would not be terribly significant because the k8s api client keeps all watched objects in a local cache (e.g. services, endpoints). IOW, coredns doesn't need to go back to the API for those requests, it just looks up the objects in a local indexed store.  For that matter - cache misses due to expired cache for kubernetes domain records is also not a big performance hit, for the same reason. So the "performance" reason for moving fro 5s to 30s in the first place is probably not as compelling as it would seem.

Thanks @chrisohaver !
Are you suggesting that moving back to 5s is maybe a better way forward?

> Thanks @chrisohaver !
> Are you suggesting that moving back to 5s is maybe a better way forward?

I am leaning that way. On the other hand, in node local deployments the response cache resides on the local node coredns instances, and the object cache resides in the cluster dns deployment. Which means a node local instance forwards misses to the cluster DNS deployment instead of just handling it internally. i.e. k8s record misses cost more in a node local deployment.

It seems that the primary reason for moving from 5s to 30s was ...

> ...  just use 30s because kube-dns has used it for a long time and seems no big complaint yet.

~... I don't _think_ there was any empirical case for the change.~

**Edit:** Strike that - It was indirectly stated that this caused a [100X](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/76238#issuecomment-481307933) performance improvement in a case.

> On the other hand, in node local deployments the response cache resides on the local node coredns instances, and the object cache resides in the cluster dns deployment. Which means a node local instance forwards misses to the cluster DNS deployment instead of just handling it internally. i.e. k8s record misses cost more in a node local deployment.

That's correct. In NodeLocalDNS, we keep the NXDOMAIN ttl to 5s. It is a small value and would cause a bunch of searchpath expanded and AAAA records to get forwarded to k8s cluster DNS, but it is somewhat of a balance between caching NXDOMAINs and discarding temporary NXDOMAINs for services whose records are being created.

> That's correct. In NodeLocalDNS, we keep the NXDOMAIN ttl to 5s. It is a small value and would cause a bunch of searchpath expanded and AAAA records to get forwarded to k8s cluster DNS, but it is somewhat of a balance between caching NXDOMAINs and discarding temporary NXDOMAINs for services whose records are being created.

IIRC, the node local Corefile has a separate server block for `cluster.local.` (or whatever the cluster's DNS suffix happens to be).  This allows for a separate cache configuration for cluster records vs records from upstream sources.

Whereas in the Cluster DNS Corefile, there is a single server block for `.` (re: [due to the way CoreDNS handles plugin chains](https://github.com/coredns/deployment/issues/153)). With a single cache, all responses (cluster domain _and_ upstream) are subject to the same cache setting.

I guess at this point, changing the defaults isn't really something that is guaranteed to be a win, but rather, just a decision that will trade one outcome for another.  I suspect by decreasing cache times:
- https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/91236 <- issues like this might get *worse* (large scalability tests overloading coredns) (note originally typo here, I wrote "better" :)) 
- issues for new apps/databases/consensus seeking pods are going to get *better*. 

1) Do we feel like there's enough variability in opinions and history here that its not a black and white solution until we collect more data, and write up an actual proposal / demo for sig-network to decide on the ideal defaults ?    I'm open to pursuing this to its logical endpoint if @dvaldivia wants to collaborate (it would be a decent time investment on both sides, though).

2) If *not* , should we simply close this and update the docs ?

Either way im open to , but just thinking at this point - since there's no *obvious* bug here, we're going to have to dig pretty deep to revert this number again, and that's only possible if we are really sure that we want to put the time/resources into making a data-driven case for it.

I was thinking the other day that the previous `kube-dns` had a nice model to injecting new DNS configurations into the cluster via a a config map, why not grab inspiration from this previous approach (and ingress) and come up with a new Resource to be able to customize the DNS? just throwing this out there for feedback

@jayunit100 I'm down to collaborate in whatever means necessary, either by figuring out healthy defaults, documenting or working on code changes if needed.

> I was thinking the other day that the previous kube-dns had a nice model to injecting new DNS configurations into the cluster via a a config map, why not grab inspiration from this previous approach (and ingress) and come up with a new Resource to be able to customize the DNS? just throwing this out there for feedback

CoreDNS is also configurable via ConfigMap.  If the default configurations do not suit a particular deployment, they can be altered.

True but adding a single stub domain cannot be done so easily, since the Corefile has some Config that needs to be parsed or manually edited.

For applications that need to add something to CoreDNS they could simply include a resource in their yaml that adds a studDomain for example and some internal controller would rebuild the Corefile configuration and apply it. I like this since this resource can be RBACed. 

Right now customers get nervous when I tell them that for my operator to work faster I need them to tweak a ConfigMap on the kube-system namespace :P

For any time travelers from the future, this issue is caused by the CoreDNS component of kube-dns, when they switched from dnsmasq to CoreDNS, they introduce a caching for misses, which lasts 30 seconds, thus the problem described above, solution is to bring your own DNS, or change the CoreDNS settings so the cache of the misses is not as long

This issue hit us in RabbitMQ multiple times:

* https://github.com/rabbitmq/cluster-operator/issues/958
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/cluster-operator/issues/269
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/cluster-operator/issues/752#issuecomment-872118881
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/cluster-operator/issues/298#issuecomment-760153567
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/issues/5322

The [rabbitmq/cluster-operator](https://github.com/rabbitmq/cluster-operator) creates a StatefulSet and headless Service with `publishNotReadyAddresses: true` at the same time and RabbitMQ pods will need to discover each other promptly upon Pod startup (that is they need to resolve each others' hostnames and their own hostname).

I think we should re-open this issue because, after 2 years have passed, there is still no good solution to this CoreDNS bug.
Some proposed solutions / workarounds that were mentioned are:

1. "Query the Kubernetes API directly (for example, using a watch) rather than relying on DNS lookups." as mentioned in the [docs](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/22446/files) is highly inconvenient for some StatefulSet Data Services. They should be able to rely on DNS and shouldn't be aware that they run on K8s. (For example in RabbitMQ, although there is a [dedicated Kubernetes peer discovery plugin](https://www.rabbitmq.com/cluster-formation.html#peer-discovery-k8s), in other Erlang code places during RabbitMQ node startup, we rely on [Erlang Port Mapper Daemon](https://www.erlang.org/doc/man/epmd.html) to resolve correctly via DNS.)
1. "Decrease the time of caching in your Kubernetes DNS provider (typically this means editing the config map for CoreDNS, which currently caches for 30 seconds)." is recommended in the [docs](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/pull/22446/files). (a) Any StatefulSet Data Service relying on discovering Pods promptly will need to document this to their users (e.g. as done [here](https://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-website/commit/4993b92c6f33446f50da9e021955c3e9aba3f4dc) for RabbitMQ) (b) Changing this global cache value such that 1 StatefulSet Data Service comes up correctly doesn't sound right. (c) I'm not sure whether all users who deploy Data Service Operators are allowed to change DNS settings in the `kube-system` namespace. 
1. Use the [CoreDNS Operator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cluster-addons/tree/master/coredns#coredns-operator). This operator is in alpha stage, and not recommended for production.

Therefore, the most appropriate current workaround is to wait in the Stateful Data Service until DNS resolution works.

In RabbitMQ this was implemented for example in:
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/pull/4233
* https://github.com/rabbitmq/rabbitmq-server/pull/2722

If DNS resolution does still not work after a few retries and up to 30 seconds, the Data Service start up will fail. This is also a poor workaround because (a) it doesn't allow to differentiate between a real DNS issue and just an outdated cache, and (b) what happens if someone configured their CoreDNS cache TTL to a value considerably higher than the default of 30 second?

Looking at the CoreDNS [code](https://github.com/coredns/coredns/blob/master/plugin/kubernetes/controller.go), it seems that CoreDNS already watches Pods, Services, and Endpoints.

As written in https://github.com/coredns/coredns/issues/2434#issuecomment-451538364:
> If you are creating the headless service at the same time as creating the pods that it selects, it will take some time for the pods to spin up and be ready. But once the pods are ready, coredns is updated almost instantaneously.

My question is:
If you are creating the headless service with `publishNotReadyAddresses: true` at the same time as creating the pods that it selects, why can't CoreDNS (cache) be updated instantaneously when a new Pod gets created? Is there any technical limitation to this solution?

if the CoreDNS cache plugin has a mechanism to invalidate cache for a particular domain which belongs to a service with `publishNotReadyAddresses: true` then we are good to go, we would only need k8s to tell CoreDNS to invalidate any cached value as soon as a pod comes online and gets an internal IP address and there wouldn't be a need to turn off the 30 seconds caching for everyone

> if the CoreDNS cache plugin has a mechanism to invalidate cache for a particular domain which belongs to a service with publishNotReadyAddresses: true then we are good to go

It does not have such a mechanism.  But IMO there is a simpler solution: if we could disable caching of records in the kubernetes zone _without_ disabling caching of upstream responses.  I have recently opened a PR to make this possible coredns/coredns#5540.

Disabling the cache plugin for _upstream_ records is a bad idea.  Disabling the cache plugin for Kubernetes service records is not bad, since the kubernetes plugin will still cache them.
